This is said because, for those at the initial stage of practice, one prescribes medicine in accordance with their own mental afflictions.
Thus, external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind; this concludes the demonstration of the source of the mind.

Since the nature of the mind has nothing external to it and its encompassing is all-pervasive—because the nature of "mind-only" has no external counterpart against which it could be contrasted—it is called "encompassing."
There is nothing it does not pervade.
From the Buddhas of the ten directions above, reaching to the limits of the Buddha-realm,
to the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm below, exhausting the very source of birth.
The essence of nature is without distinction;
sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual. All things are universally pervasive. This Dharma-gate of the mind-ground is the inconceivable liberation of the nature of reality.
An ancient said: "The Buddha within the minds of sentient beings is silent and still in nirvana; the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind are restless in birth and death. Truly, they are one.
All things are entirely pervasive.
Who speaks of internal and external, form and mind, self and other? When both person and phenomena have vanished, one says "who?"—for they are merged in non-duality.
Since internal and external, form and mind, self and other are all quiescent, it is said: "Who speaks of internal and external, form and mind?"
This is accomplished by means of the preceding "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind. It is called "accomplishment" because wondrous contemplation is established based on the wondrous object.

Regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature": to use wisdom to create the object is called "cultivation," while the three obstacles are called "nature. This refers to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
It is said that the constant object is signless and the constant wisdom is without an object. Although wisdom has no object, it constantly gives rise to the object;
although the object is signless, it constantly serves as the condition for wisdom. Because the signless object lacks signs, the signs of wisdom arise from its manifestation.

"Manifestation" means the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because wisdom without an object takes a signless object as its condition, this very condition is "creation"; "creation" means non-existence.
The non-duality of appearance and reality, as well as object and wisdom, constitutes the gate of cultivation and nature.

The nature-virtues are nothing other than the single thought-moment of the dharma-realm. Referring back to the section on the mind and form above, the totality of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses within a single thought-moment is discussed solely in terms of nature-virtues; this is termed the "objective realm of principle" (li-jing).
This internal realm is fully endowed with three dharmas. This "internal" refers to a single thought-moment; "realm" refers to a hundred realms; and "suchness" refers to a thousand suchnesses.
These three dharmas are fully present. Briefly, within these three dharmas there are ten kinds of triple dharmas—namely, the path, consciousness, nature, and so forth.
Extensively, they comprise immeasurable triple dharmas. As the Great Master Fu said: "The salty taste within water; the glue within color."
The blue is definitively existent; though its form is not seen, it is truly said that every gate is complete and every dharma is perfectly accomplished.
Relying on wisdom, one gives rise to cultivation. "Relying" means to depend upon wisdom to open up the provisional and the real, as in the four teachings within the wondrous Middle Way. II.

The first three of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) in the provisional teachings comprise sixteen knowledges and constitute the provisional; the four knowledges in the Perfect Teaching constitute the real. As the Sūtra says:
"If I were to praise the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would have no way to attain true knowledge.

Reflecting upon the Buddhas of the past, [the Bodhisattva] realizes that they all used the power of skillful means (*upāya*) to teach and transform sentient beings. Thus he reflects: "The Buddhas of the ten directions praise [this]."
To implement the provisional [teachings], one first bestows the three baskets (*piṭaka*) and the seven wisdoms of arising and ceasing;
subsequently, as the provisional and the real are mutually correlated, it was necessary to wait more than forty years before the real wisdom was opened to reveal the original realm.

Because the three dharmas are fully present therein, it is said that "one relies on wisdom to initiate cultivation. The scriptural passages cited above accord with the principle of "resonance between like sounds," and their underlying meaning is thus clearly elucidated.
However, one need not harbor doubts regarding the question: "The four teachings and twenty wisdoms were spoken by the Buddha;

how can it be said that the teachings give rise to practice through the medium of wisdom? Answer: It is precisely because the teachings are the words of the supreme sages directed toward those below, and sentient beings receive these teachings according to their capacity for the provisional and the real.
Within the ultimate teaching, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are revealed, and thus one gives rise to practice in accordance with reality.

Although the nature of clouds is inherently thus, it is only through relying on wisdom that cultivation arises. The ancient text reads "relying on wisdom to initiate cultivation" (籍智起修); the reading "relying on wisdom to cultivate" (籍智修) is an error.
Some interpret "wisdom" as "numinous awareness" (靈知), but they have misunderstood the meaning of "wisdom."

By cultivating the nature of illumination: this means that while the reality is ultimate, it is provisionally opened through skillful means. As the scripture says: "If the Kunlun bamboo is not yet trimmed, the phoenix’s song will not manifest;
if the nature is not yet refined, the divine spirit will not emerge. Therefore, it is said: "by cultivating the nature of illumination."

Cultivation is initiated by nature; the provisional and the real are fused, and nature points to the three obstacles. Since cultivation is perfected through nature, it is said that "cultivation is initiated by nature.
When one abides in nature, cultivation is entirely perfected as nature. As the text below states: "The three thousand [realms] existing within principle are collectively termed ignorance."
In cultivation, the nature is fully realized as cultivation. As the subsequent text states: "When the three thousand [realms] are perfected as fruit, they are all termed eternal and blissful.
The nature does not shift; as stated below: "The three thousand are unchanging."
Cultivation remains ever-vivid. As the subsequent text states: "Ignorance is itself clarity.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of cultivation: the cultivation that reveals the provisional and the real, and the cultivation that follows or opposes [the teaching]. That which refers to the teachings of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*) is called "contrary cultivation" (*pratiloma-bhāvanā*); that which refers to the Mahāyāna of complete meaning (*nītārtha*) is called "concordant cultivation" (*anuloma-bhāvanā*).

"Conformity" refers to practicing by realizing one's nature; for without a mind that flows from the Truth, there is no way to accord with the Truth—how then could the practice of true cultivation not arise from the Truth?

"Rebellion" refers to turning one's back on one's nature to create delusion; to extinguish the mind in search of the Way while following the practices of the Three Teachings is to be confused and deluded.
The True Perfect Person alone is called the Elder Who Has Realized Nature (Liaoxing Zhangzhe). He said:

"If one realizes that the dependent origination of a single thought-moment is unborn, one transcends the provisional teachings and dualistic views of the Three Vehicles; how could this not be called 'conforming' to the realization of nature as practice?

Thus we know that the provisional teachings involve "contrary cultivation," and their conformity or contrariness can be understood by way of their flavor (*rasa*) and their divisions (*nikāya*). Some take the six realms of existence to be...

To take the four teachings practiced in reverse order as those practiced in direct order shows a failure to understand the distinction between the inverse and the direct. Since the six realms are fundamentally the three obstructions, what is there to be cultivated?
As the following text states, "One should know that 'nature' refers to the three obstructions," which makes this clear.
Regarding the two aspects of delusion and awakening, although the mind itself is non-dual, the natures of delusion and awakening are like space, fundamentally non-dual.

Yet, the two natures of contrariness and conformity are eternally distinct in their characteristics and phenomena. "Nature" refers to the nature of grasping; because of grasping, phenomena are established. Thus, they share the same nature.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Because the nature of the mind is luminous and the mind-nature is perfectly bright, based on this luminosity, the nature gives rise to [perception], and from this, deluded vision arises.

From that which is ultimately non-existent, there is established what is ultimately existent. 'Based on luminosity, the nature gives rise to [perception]'—'arising' (fa) refers to the capacity to perceive objects;
because the deluded mind does not understand, it forms attachments to the nature. As for 'phenomena,' their characteristics are mutually contradictory."

It is said: "The 'ever-distinct' refers to the nature of clinging; because this nature of clinging and the aforementioned nature of the mind share the same principle but differ in their functions, they are distinguished as 'contrary' and 'conformable.
Since both the nature and the phenomena are ever-distinct, it can be seen that the causes and effects of the ten realms, including both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, are inextricably diverse."

If one does not shift the mind from the phenomenal reality (*dharma*), it will cause confusion regarding the realization of cultivation and completion. The Japanese commentary states that this intends to negate false conceptualization (*vikalpa*):

"Is it possible that because one does not shift the true mind from the phenomena of birth and death, one instead clings to them and becomes confused regarding the realization of cultivation and completion?

In principle, confusion and realization must be utterly distinct in their characteristics, as they are both the natural truth (*t'ien-chên*). Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Both are extinguished; they are pure."
The *Guangdashi* commentary states: "To conclude with the meaning of *liqù* (principle-trend):

because the emotional and cognitive measures of both ordinary beings and sages are all but mere traces, and because the nature of phenomena—whether in accord or in opposition—is severed from the true source, it is called *liqù*. *Liqù* means that which is *dharmatā* (the natural state of things)."

Therefore, within a single period, one must extinguish both the deluded and the enlightened, so that the illuminating nature becomes cultivation and the seeing of nature merges with the cultivation of the mind; thus, both minds are utterly stilled.
"Therefore, it is necessary" (*hèxū*) is a term used to introduce the subject. "A single period" (*yīqī*) refers to the teachings of the Dharma during a single lifetime.

"Deluded and enlightened" (*míliao*) means that the provisional teachings are called "deluded," while the definitive Mahāyāna is called "enlightened. Within these two categories of teaching—both the deluded and the enlightened—there exists...

Regarding the statement that "illuminating the nature accomplishes cultivation" (*zhào xìng chéng xiū*) and "seeing the nature cultivates the mind" (*jiàn xìng xiū xīn*), the *Yì* (Commentary) says: "Illuminating the nature accomplishes cultivation" is largely feared to refer to cultivation based on conditions (*yuán xiū*).

Because one cultivates by taking the True as the object-condition (*yuán zhēn ér xiū*), it is called "illuminating the nature accomplishes cultivation. "Seeing the nature cultivates the mind" refers to true cultivation (*zhēn xiū*). The meaning is that [the former] is cultivation based on conditions and the True;

illuminating the nature and seeing the nature have not yet transcended relativity (*jué dài*), and the state of duality (*duì dài*) has not yet been extinguished. Thus, the mind has not yet been lost.
Contemplating how to sever desire and manifest the sublime essence, it is said that "the two minds are both extinguished.
This means that seeing the nature is the seeing of one who practices through faith, while illuminating the nature is the illumination of one who practices through dharma.

Both the accomplishment of cultivation and the cultivation of the mind are the principles of contemplative cultivation; because these are utterly severed within the midst of principle, they are called "both extinguished."
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Realizing that the nature of cultivation is non-dual, there is only the single wondrous vehicle;

the dharma-realm is transparently luminous and free from discrimination, such that the ultimate and conventional truths are non-dual. Do not harbor further doubts regarding these characters of a single period [of teaching]; those who continue to doubt them can do nothing about it.
In the ancient edition, the character "one" (*ichi*) was used instead of "its" (*shitsu*); this more clearly manifests the wondrous meaning. Some have said: "One..."
Those who are deluded do not understand this. The ancient text reads "the two cultivations are both extinguished," yet even this meaning has no fixed basis.

This is because when both the provisional cultivation and the true cultivation are extinguished, there is nothing to differentiate. Some say that the six realms are "contrary cultivation" and the four teachings are "conformable cultivation";
only when these two types of cultivation are extinguished can one be said to have seen one's nature—this refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
It is excellent that this person does not see nature as being "perfect" (yuan).

Furthermore, one must understand that in accordance with cultivation, there is both separation from and union with nature. The preceding passage cited the general purport of the teachings throughout the entire dispensation, hence it said "one period" (yiqi);

this [present passage], however, specifically highlights the characteristics of the separation and union of cultivation and nature within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), hence it says "furthermore, one must understand."
"Separation" refers to the threefold nature of each of the two—cultivation and essence. Regarding the three aspects of cultivation, the *Wenju* states: "The Dharma-body, wisdom, and abandonment;
the Dharma-body is the Dharma-body virtue within cultivation, wisdom is the Prajñā virtue within cultivation, and abandonment is the liberation virtue within cultivation.

Regarding the three aspects of essence, the *Wenju* states: "The true-mark, merit, and function; the true-mark is the Dharma-body virtue within essence. As for "merit," it refers to the merit within essence.

It is clear that the two characters "virtue" (*de*) refer to the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation within the nature (*xing*). If, in the context of cultivation (*xiu*), they were further separated as in the following passage, it would be so;
however, their unification means that the two [cultivations] are one with the nature. The cultivation of the two refers to the cultivation of the two virtues of *prajñā* and liberation.
Regarding "the perfection of the nature as one": this means that the single virtue of the *dharmakāya* is inherently present within the nature.
Regarding "the two aspects of cultivation, each with three": *prajñā* and liberation are the two virtues of cultivation, each having three aspects.
Within *prajñā*, the three are: the *dharmakāya* is the *prajñā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*), while contemplation is the *prajñā* of observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).
The *prajñā* within that [liberation] is the *prajñā* of the syllables; liberation within *prajñā* consists of three aspects:
the liberation of pure nature is the *dharmakāya* within liberation;
the liberation of perfect purity is the *prajñā* within liberation; and the liberation of skillful means is the [liberation] within liberation.
Liberation (*vimukti*) is likewise each threefold; this further elaborates upon the qualities of cultivation mentioned in the preceding text.
Regarding the three natures that arise together: the nature of suffering is the *dharmakāya*; the nature of afflictions is *prajñā*;
and the nature of karma is liberation.

Thus, although cultivation (bhāvanā) comprises nine aspects, when cultivation and nature (prakṛti) are contrasted, they are distinguished into nine kinds; yet when considered in relation to one another, these nine are collectively termed cultivation.
These nine are merely three, for the three natures are the foundation that subsumes cultivation back into nature. By unifying function with essence, essence and function are not sequential.
There are not merely three virtues individually;
rather, because cultivation is presented in contrast to the nature (prakṛti), cultivation is combined into two categories.

Within the category of combined cultivation, the three types of *prajñā* constitute one virtue of *prajñā*, and the three types of liberation (*vimokṣa*) within combined cultivation constitute one virtue of liberation; therefore, it is called "combined cultivation."

Although cultivation consists of two virtues, these are nonetheless accomplished through the nature; thus, they are not distinct from it. Although the nature is one, the three virtues are perfectly manifest;
yet, they are also not separate from one another.
Within the teaching that unifies cultivation and nature, the three virtues are explained as being integrated within the single nature.
It is like water forming waves. Water is a metaphor for the single quality of the Dharmakāya within the nature; waves are a metaphor for the two qualities cultivated—prajñā and liberation.
These two are also non-dual. Within the cultivated qualities, these two are likewise non-dual; prajñā and liberation are fundamentally one.

The principle of cultivation in relation to its nature is called "two," yet it is also "not two. Because water and waves are not two—cultivation and nature being as one—it is said that they are both "two" and "not two.
Furthermore, just as waves are water, when both cultivation and nature are extinguished, it is called "inconceivable," like waves being water.
First, as for who speaks of "cultivation" and "nature":
one should know that "nature" refers to the three obstacles—the obstacle of suffering, the obstacle of afflictions, and the obstacle of karma. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The primordially abiding dharma (bennǜ fǎ) is ineffable."

Therefore, all three are complete. Among the ten sets of three dharmas, the first three—the three natures—refer to the three paths; they exist by the very nature of reality (dharmatā) from the beginning.
Cultivation is accomplished through these natures, for cultivation is brought forth by means of the natures.

The accomplishment of the three dharmas as their natural state (*dharmatā*) refers to ascending to the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching], which is called the "wonderfulness of the three dharmas" because they are not separate from the three paths of ordinary beings.
Since the body of wisdom possessed therein is clearly manifest and realized without depending on others, it is said that "the three dharmas are accomplished as their natural state."
One realizes that there is neither the nature of cultivation nor the waves and water;
there is only the single wondrous vehicle. As the Sūtra says: "In all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle, without any differentiation.
Here, seeing and hearing are cut off from principle, and the Way transcends thought and deliberation.

The Dharma-realm is profoundly luminous; in every phenomenon, there is non-obstruction, and the imperial net of the Dharma-realm unfolds in successive layers, such that the three thousand natures and appearances are ultimately and naturally radiant.

This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of internal and external. Because the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature is established from the standpoint of object and wisdom, it is said:
The gate of the non-duality of the internal and external is thus established.
Regarding the fourth gate, the non-duality of cause and effect, the Commentary states: "In the Mahāyāna, the cause is the true aspect (dharmatā), and the fruit is the true aspect;
since both are the true aspect, their non-duality is evident."
Regarding the causes of the minds of sentient beings: the three thousand realms existing within principle are collectively termed ignorance as the cause.
Since they fully possess the three tracks—the track of true nature, the track of contemplative illumination, and the track of material support—the three dharmas within the causal state are wondrous.
When these causes result in fruition, they are called the three types of nirvana: first, the nirvana of intrinsic purity; second, the nirvana of perfected purity;

and third, the nirvana of purity through skillful means. These three dharmas within the fruition are wondrous, and as the fruit of the three thousand realms is accomplished, they are all termed "eternal" and "blissful."
Cause and effect are not distinct; the principle of beginning and end is one. Since the cause is the beginning and the fruit is the end, their underlying principle is non-dual.

If this is so, since the qualities are already complete within the cause, why does it not abide in the cause? This interrogates: since the three qualities are already fully present within the cause, what need is there to proceed toward the fruit of nirvana?
It is solely due to delusion regarding the cause. The answer addresses the universal delusion concerning the three internal dharmas, which are fundamentally wondrous;

each regards itself as real. "Regards" (wei) refers to grasping and conceptualization. As the treatise states: "When sentiment arises, wisdom is obstructed; when perception changes, the substance becomes distinct.
'Real' refers to the attachment to reality."
If one thoroughly understands the nature of delusion—"thoroughly" meaning to penetrate—then one penetrates that the essence of delusion is fundamentally wondrous.
It is truly only the causal basis for abiding. "Truly" means that this is the ultimate reality; as a sutra says, "bondage and liberation share the same source."

Therefore, having long investigated this cause, the manifestation of the cause is called the fruit. By contemplating and analyzing the cause until its manifestation, one sees that it is precisely the fruit.
This is solely because the principle of cause and fruit is one; thus, the subtle thesis is established and demonstrated.
Taking this single principle as the cause, the Sūtra says: "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas.
Since the principle is now manifest, the name of the fruit no longer exists; how could the designation of the cause still persist? Thus, the three thousand marks are extinguished.
Rationality vanishes of its own accord. As stated above, when both the mind that perceives nature and the mind that cultivates the mind are extinguished, it is solely due to the forgetting of wisdom.
The Sūtra says: "When ignorance ceases, the objects produced by illumination vanish; once the objects established by illumination are gone, the nature of illumination itself is forgotten."
Regarding intimacy and estrangement: to point to a stranger as father and son is intimacy; to point to father and son as strangers is estrangement.

This causes one to become deluded regarding the depth or shallowness [of relationships]. To take the cessation of the mind as the Way is to be deluded about what is deep; to take the mind itself as the Way is to be deluded about what is shallow.
Because delusion varies in its density, the three afflictions are forcibly distinguished; though they are not actually divided, to divide them is what is meant by "forcibly.

In terms of meaning, this opens up the six stages of identity (*liù jí*). Because cause and effect share a single principle, they are called "identity" (*jí*, pronounced with a departing tone). Since ordinary beings and sages do not overlap, they are designated as "six" (*liù*, also pronounced with a departing tone).

This refers to the relative depth and shallowness of wisdom. Regarding the three wisdoms—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*)—their relative depth and shallowness are discussed in mutual relation.

Thus, "exerting oneself as if in a dream" is used; "dreamer" is the metaphor for the person, "sleep" is the metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*), and the phenomena of the dream are the metaphor for the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages.

The nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is likened to the person, while ignorance is likened to sleep; the causes and effects of both mundane and supramundane realms are likened to the events within the dream. The adornment [of the path] is likewise explained.
The dream of Zhou Mengdie is a dream-event within the nature; the ten-faith bodhisattvas dreaming of manifesting the eight phases of Buddhahood is a dream-event of semblance.
The first-stage bodhisattva, having for the first time shattered ignorance, is like awakening from a dream; only when ultimate perfect enlightenment is reached does the dream finally end.
Now it is clarified that, in discussing the fifty-two stages shared by both ordinary beings and sages, their progression is like a single dream.
The dream-phenomena seen therein arise precisely because inconceivable karma transforms what is unreal; thus they are like a dream.
For a practitioner who possesses faith and follows the teachings by means of contemplation without interruption from moment to moment, it is said that they "apply themselves with diligence."
It is empty and dark. Because fundamental ignorance has no self-nature, it is called "empty"; because even this characteristic of emptiness is empty, it is called "dark.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "Being unstained yet stained is difficult to comprehend; being stained yet unstained is difficult to comprehend. A sūtra says:
"Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. It further says:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single speck of cloud appearing against the vast azure. It further states:
"Awakened clarity and the dullness of emptiness. The *Lun* (Treatise) says that "the empty Tathāgata-garbha" refers to the fact that what falsely arises has no substance, and is thus called "empty.

Therefore, it is evident that the textual evidence for the dictionary definition of "emptiness" (*kōng*) as "dark and profound stillness" is clearly trustworthy. Furthermore, it is said that this character "empty" (*kōng*) is...
"Metaphor" (*yu*) means "obscuration. In the ancient edition, it was written as "name" (*mingzi*), which is a shallow interpretation.

When delusion is severed—since the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is already darkened, the delusions of its branches and twigs are naturally severed—it is said that "emptiness is dark and delusion is severed.

The meaning intended by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) lies in the inconceivable nature of these delusions; that is, the fundamental ignorance itself is not something to be removed gradually, and thus the metaphor is like this.

When smelting iron, the coarse impurities fall away first; likewise, from the initial stage of faith, the five abodes are completely subdued. From the first faith up to the seventh faith, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) fall away first.

Thus, there is a semblance of the true cause, and through these stages, wisdom is perfected. This also forcefully distinguishes the meaning of the three delusions, opening them into the six stages of realization (*ṣat-avasthā*).
The original intent is that the afflictions of the five abodes are themselves the true nature (*tathatā*), and thus there is no higher stage [beyond this].
Because the true and the semblance, as well as the ordinary and the sage, are each distinct, the fifty-two stages of the true and the semblance are like dreams and illusions.
When the causes of illusion are fulfilled, "the illusionist" is a metaphor; because the cause of ignorance is unreal, it is like an illusion. As the *Sūtra* says:
"It is like a skillful illusionist who conjures various men and women; although one sees their various faculties move, they are actually drawn by a single mechanism."

Ceasing the workings of the mind, one returns to the fundamental source, whereby all illusions are realized as being without intrinsic nature. That "single working" is ignorance (*avidyā*). Because ignorance has no inherent nature, the eternal principle is revealed.
Among the four teachings, in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) Teaching, there is "sentimental wisdom": "sentimental" refers to abiding in the reality-limit while remaining unaware that it is an illusion.
Those of the *Tong* (Shared) Teaching merely penetrate the illusory phenomena; those of the *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching penetrate the illusionist.
Those who do not understand that illusory phenomena are the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are not only ignorant of the illusion itself;

they fail to realize that both the illusionist and the illusory phenomena constitute the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Furthermore, because the application of contemplation has not yet reached its conclusion, that which is non-illusory appears as illusory.

Therefore, from the stage of the Five Ranks and the Ten Faiths up to Equal Enlightenment (*samāyikabodhi*), all are termed "illusory causes" (*māyā-hetu*), for although they possess illusion, [they are ultimately non-illusory].

Even at the stage of fruition, as long as one has not yet reached the ultimate, it is still called "initial enlightenment" (*shijue*); only upon reaching the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miaojue*) is it said that the illusory cause is fully perfected.
This was the original intent of Tiantai: that the causal stage of the first dwelling is itself the true cause, while the ultimate fruition of Wondrous Enlightenment is the true fruit;
only then does the name "illusory" come to an end.
The "resultant fruit of the mirror-image" is perfected. The *Treatise* states: "When initial enlightenment merges with fundamental enlightenment, they are equal and equal;
equal and equal. These four repetitions refer to the inconceivable fruit. At this time, the physical body manifests within the ten dharma-realms;
this is precisely the ultimate Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies. Because it is like a mirror manifesting images, it is called the "mirror-image."
"Result" (*phala*) refers to perfection.

Although "emptiness" (*śūnya*) and "image" (*bimba*) are identical in meaning, the deluded mind has no substance and is thus called "empty," while the physical body has form and is thus called an "image.

Furthermore, the true mind is without marks and is thus called "empty," yet its manifested forms are not void and are thus called "images. Since both are subsumed within a single thought-moment, they are said to be identical in meaning.

The same applies here. Yet, while the void is empty, the image is real. Master Min said: "Delusion is not delusion because it is the source of delusion; truth is not truth because it is the thought of truth.

Therefore, it is called the "Discourse on Emptiness and Voidness. The *Zhishen lun* (Treatise on the Body of Wisdom) states: "The body of wisdom is vast and expansive, taking the myriad images as its physical form and the hundred realms [as its substance]."
Because it manifests as a form, it is called a "phenomenal reality" (xiangshi);

because it is a phenomenal reality, it is said to accord with the principle that [the three thousand realms] are primordially existent. As the subsequent text states: "Within emptiness, the provisional [three thousand realms] are perfectly manifest," and thus it is said they accord with the principle that they are primordially existent.
Because it is empty and void, delusion transforms into the nature (*xing*). "Nature" refers to the true nature;

because one cultivates that which is not cultivated, the original meaning—that delusion originally transforms into the nature—is that the nature itself does not require further cultivation to be realized. Thus, one knows that the two characters "empty" (*kōng*) and "void" (*xū*) in the preceding passage are not erroneous.
Please observe the phrase "because it is empty and void, delusion transforms [into] the nature," and its meaning will become self-evident.
Thus, where there is non-duality, duality arises; cause and effect become entangled, establishing a distinction between them.
This concludes the demonstration of why duality exists.
Two yet not two. This principle is the primordial true reality (*dharmatā*).
From beginning to end, its essence is one; the essence of cause and effect is fundamentally one from start to finish.

If one were to claim that the cause differs from the effect, then the cause would not truly be a cause. In both the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings, the cause and effect differ; in the *Bie* (Separate) Teaching, they are distinct.

Because the cause is impermanent while the fruit is permanent, because the cause does not proceed toward the merit of the fruit, and because the fruit does not encompass the cause, it is said that the cause differs from the fruit, and thus the cause is not [truly] a cause.

To understand that the fruit arises from the cause: the beginner of the Perfect Person understands that the fruit arises from the cause, meaning that the reality of cause and fruit is obtained through the cause.
Because the fruit is also a real fruit, it is said that one understands the fruit as arising from causes;
the cause must first produce the fruit. Just as a current flows toward the sea, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not stop.
Thus, the "three thousand" [phenomena] existing within the principle are collectively termed ignorance; this is the actual cause.
When the three thousandfold world-systems have reached fruition, they are all called "Eternal and Blissful"; this is the true fruit.
The three thousandfold world-systems undergo no change, for their nature is immutable.
Ignorance is itself enlightenment; the cultivation of the eternal remains perfectly intact.
The three thousand realms are both in essence and in function, eternally co-present. As the preceding text states: "Creation refers to essence and function;

the Dharma-gate of the Tiantai Mind-Ground and its inconceivable liberation are attained by both ordinary beings and sages. This function allows a mustard seed to contain Mount Sumeru and a single hair to conceal the vast ocean.
Pei Xiu even remarked: "To cast the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters is merely our ordinary allotment. Thus it is said.
Why do you so painfully cling to the identity of substance? How could their functions not be different?

Even the ancients said that the rites for which there were no teachers were not fabricated by the Duke of Zhou or Confucius, and that the wisdom for which there were no teachers was not bestowed by the Buddhas;
how much more so when it comes to the white talismans and the discussion of the mind—how can one be so utterly ignorant of this? How extreme this is!
This is established by the Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature, which concludes by demonstrating the objective realm and wisdom upon which cause and effect depend.
Regarding the fifth, the Gate of the Non-duality of Defilement and Purity: ignorance is defilement and the nature of reality (dharmatā) is purity;
these are two in their mutual dependence, yet they are non-dual because they share a single principle as their gate. Thus it is called "non-dual."
If consciousness has been without beginning, then because the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) constitutes ignorance, one can now understand that ignorance itself is the *dharmatā*.
The *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "The pure Tathāgatagarbha and the worldly Ālayavijñāna are like gold fashioned into a ring;
they are indistinguishable throughout their transformation. If one understands this, it is true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*); those with corrupt wisdom (*ku-prajñā*) cannot know the Garbha.
Because it can be understood through the *ālayavijñāna*, the "store" (*ālaya*) is itself consciousness.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) universally produce all dharmas; this is termed "defilement. Although undefiled, it is defiled.

The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* clarifies the six types of defilement, while the Tiantai school speaks of the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*), and the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* (or *Dharmadhātu-prakṛti-śāstra*) clarifies that defilement is the basis [of purity]. Therefore, it is said:
The nine aspects of arising and ceasing are termed "conditioning" because they pertain to the characteristics of birth and death.
Ignorance and the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), which universally respond to all conditions, are termed "purity. As that *Sūtra on the Exposition of Attainment* says:
"O sons of the Buddha who possess virtue, from the time I was an ordinary person bound by all fetters, I have passed through all stages and perfected the causes of practice."
The Ocean Adornment, the Great Awakening Fruit: I have traversed all stages from the Ground of Purity;

having perfected all myriad practices, I attained the foremost stage of faith and entered the ocean of the storehouse of ignorance. Thus, these two great matters occur simultaneously without priority or sequence.

In the state of defilement, they are called "creation"; in the state of purity, they are called "response. Although their names and forms differ, if one observes the original intent of the text, they are fundamentally one.

That is to say, within the single principle of dependent origination, the nature of inconceivable liberation naturally branches into various paths, all of which take *tathatā* (suchness) as their locus;
thus one may speak of "two dharma-gates" being simultaneous and without sequence.
The meaning of the following metaphor clearly reveals the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.

Turbid water and clear water are no different in their wetness. Master Mi said that the nature of wetness being no different can be used as a metaphor for the fact that sentient beings and Buddhas share the same true nature;
thus it is called "identical substance. While there are clear waves and turbid waves, their function in irrigation and so forth is the same;

this can be used as a metaphor for the distinction between the functions of ordinary beings and sages, and the difference between birth-and-death and nirvana. Contemplate the meaning of the text according to these points.

The essence and function of both sentient beings and all Buddhas are inconceivable; since liberation is such that both essence and function are identical for both ordinary beings and sages, there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference between them. Thus it is said: "The waves and the moisture are no different."

Although clarity and turbidity arise from conditions, a water-clearing jewel can make water clear, serving as the condition for clarity, while fish and dragons agitating the water cause it to become turbid, serving as the condition for turbidity.
This means that although the essence of water is originally clear, in principle it is neither clear nor turbid;
when external conditions arrive, it becomes either clear or turbid. This may be used as a metaphor for the true nature, which is originally neither defiled nor pure.
Because the deluded mind is turbid and the understanding mind is clear, sentient beings serve as the conditions for turbidity while the Buddhas serve as the conditions for purity;
thus, it is explained that the arising of clarity depends on the sequence of sentient beings and Buddhas.

Therefore, the subsequent text reiterates: "Yet turbidity is fundamentally inherent," because although they are unstained, they become stained, and because sentient beings exist both before and after [the Buddhas], this is discussed first in the treatise.
Subsequently, although turbidity is originally present, its entire substance is pure. The fact that afflictions are originally present is analogous to sentient beings being situated in front;

thus it is said, "although turbidity is originally present. This refers to the afflictions as being identical to the nature of Bodhi, for their fundamental nature is pure; thus it is said, "its entire substance [is pure]."
This is clarity.

Because the two principles (li) universally pervade the entire substance (ti), they constitute function (yong). "Universally" means completely. What is mundane is the turbid wave; what is sagely is the clear wave.
Since the principle-substance is completely pervasive, its entire substance constitutes function. As the *Huan-yuan guan* says: "Function is the waves; the supreme cauldron [is the substance]."

The boiling [water] perfects the true substance through its operation; the substance is itself the purity of the environment. As the water clarifies, it accords with the conditions of words and circumstances to converge in stillness;
therefore, it is said that "the entire substance is function.

Thus, the three thousand [realms] of cause and effect are both termed "dependent origination" (paratantra-svabhāva). This is because cause and effect are themselves the phenomena of dependent origination.
The dependent origination of delusion and awakening does not depart from a single kṣaṇa. In Sanskrit it is called *tallapa*, which here is translated as *kṣaṇa*, meaning the shortest possible moment.
A verse says: "The mind that is but a mere *ji* (moment)"—this refers to the most subtle and faint mind.

The principle of the momentary nature and the perpetual dependent origination are one and the same. That the nature which is eternally abiding in a single thought-moment arises and ceases in every successive thought-moment is precisely because the numinous awareness is eternally abiding;
it reflects upon objects without interruption, flowing spontaneously and naturally without ceasing.
From antiquity to the present, it has never been interrupted; therefore, it is said that the momentary nature and the perpetual principle of dependent origination are one.

Within the single principle, purity and defilement are distinguished. Although the ten realms are in chaotic confusion and lack differentiation, they are distinct in their respective defilement and purity;
the three thousand realms are perfectly manifest.
As for their distinction, there are six defiled realms: the cycle of birth and death within the six paths is entirely defiled, yet therein it is not that the inherent purity is absent.

Regarding the four purities (*śuddhi*): because they are established through the severance of delusions by means of virtue and the realization of wisdom, they are provisionally termed "pure. Yet, within them, the presence of inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) is not absent.
Generally speaking, all ten [realms] encompass both the pure and the defiled; it should be understood that both purity and defilement pervade all ten realms.
Therefore, one knows that the defiled essence of every moment is entirely pure; it is fundamentally pure within its own nature.

While the three thousand [realms] have not yet manifested, perfect purity (*pariśuddhi*)—referring to the wisdom of *prajñā* in terms of cultivated virtue—is spoken of in relation to delusion and awakening.

If one’s realization of the essence remains deluded, consider this: if all that is discussed as the Three Thousand Worlds is entirely the wondrous realm, and yet the Three Thousand have not yet manifested, how can one still say that the realization of the essence is deluded?
Furthermore, how could there still be external objects to confront?

Therefore, in the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*), the six sense organs achieve universal illumination. Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the illumination through inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) is not yet perfected;
it is only upon reaching the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*) that the realization of principle is perfected, whereby one perfection entails the perfection of all.
Within this stage of semblance, the six sense organs function interchangeably, illuminating the ten realms, the ten indeterminate states, and the ten [stages of] non-determination.

The ten realms shine forth distinctly within each part; a single faculty possesses the ten dharma-realms, extending even to the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, mutually illuminating and radiantly manifest.
Thus, a single faculty possesses the five faculties; when these mutually illuminate one another, a single faculty possesses six sets of the three-thousandfold nature and characteristics.
Calculated across the six faculties, there are thirty-six sets of the three-thousandfold nature and characteristics, with each of the six faculties possessing its own.
Within each and every thought-moment, the six sense organs are each fully present in incalculable numbers;
how could one wait for the fruition of the state to equal the hundred realms? As for the subsequent mention of "the fruition equaling those hundred realms," this is merely a partial analysis.

How could those with the six sense organs purified claim that the ten [stages] are fixed as ten? As for those at the stage of the ten faiths, although they do not discuss sequential order within the midst of non-sequential progression, the fundamental intent of the textual divisions is that each and every stage contains the three thousand [worlds].

The manifestation of partial truth within the ten realms is likewise so. Regarding the statement that "for those who have attained the stages [of the Ten Abidings], their manifestation of partial true Middle Way within the ten realms is likewise so":
this means that their manifestations are identical to those prior to the stages, wherein they manifest bodies of the ten dharma-realms and the six sense organs function interdependently.

This is also consistent with the meaning of the passage which says: "Although those in the causal stage have realized partial truth to the ultimate degree, they are not yet equal to the hundred realms. Therefore, it is stated below:
When the fruition is perfected, it equals those hundred realms;
even until the fruition is perfected and equals those hundred realms, within the causal stage—where there is neither increase nor decrease—one discusses increase and decrease.

In the stages of cultivation where increase and decrease are discussed, this refers to the manifestation of the nature of the three thousand realms which was originally not yet fully realized, now being proven as the fruition.
The wondrous enlightenment is rectified and square in its nature; throughout the ten realms and their thousand suchnesses, there is neither increase nor decrease.

Therefore, from the very first thought-moment, one must both negate and illumine. That which "is not in the beginning" yet "does not depart from the beginning" means that through the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, illumination arises as a matter of course.
There being no one, two, or three is negation; the presence of one, two, and three is illumination.
Because it illuminates, the three thousand realms are eternally present; because the essence of their nature is radiant, they are said to be "eternally present.

Because it obstructs, phenomena are naturally within emptiness; just as flames directed toward the sky are extinguished by the natural law of the void, so too are all things extinguished within emptiness.

Throughout the day they are both extinguished; throughout the day they both illuminate. Because obscuring and illuminating occur simultaneously without mutual separation or distinction, it is called "throughout the day.

Without moving from this single thought, one responds universally and boundlessly. Since a single thought is the Dharma-realm, there is no shifting or displacement; yet one responds universally to all beings.
The spiritual capacity (*ki*) likewise has no fixed location;
it bestows [its response] according to what is invoked. It is like a hen brooding her chicks: the calling and the pecking occur simultaneously.
Thus, purity and impurity are both obliterated; when both essence (*xing*) and appearance (*xiang*) have perished, how could purity and impurity exist?

Because there is no distinction between the pure and the defiled, one employs emptiness and the Middle. The meaning is that by means of emptiness and the Middle, the three thousand phenomena (the *sanqian*) are merged;

yet within emptiness and the Middle, the provisional (*jia*) three thousand phenomena are perfectly manifest. Therefore, from the first thought-moment (*ādikṣaṇa*), one must both negate and illumine, until reaching the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), which is not different from the nature of the first thought-moment.
This is because the fundamental nature of reality is thus; even if one practices, it is likewise so. This is exclusively the Perfect [Teaching], and it is most difficult and most profound.
It is difficult [to realize that] phenomena are by their very nature quiescent from the beginning; Yongjia said, "Liberation and quiescence are the Dharmakāya.

Nevertheless, it is through emptiness that the defiled is transformed into the pure, and the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms, all because of the transformation of the defiled basis (*āśraya*).

Through the realization of defilement and purity, both defilement is seen as not defiled and purity as not pure; by cultivating contemplation upon these objects, defilement and purity vanish of their own accord within emptiness.
Thus, mind and phenomena both perish, and medicine and illness are simultaneously extinguished.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect; that defilement and purity do not transcend cause and effect brings the intended meaning back to the fundamental source.

Regarding the sixth gate, the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*): among the three thousand aspects, one thousand are the lands where beings dwell, termed the "environment" (*niśraya*), and two thousand are the realms of those who dwell therein, termed the "inhabitants" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because they are all subsumed within a single thought-moment, they are called non-dual; this is the identity of the container and the contained.
These serve as the gates through which one penetrates.

Having realized that the *dharmadhātu* (the all-encompassing void) and the *tathatā* (suchness) are of one essence and non-dual—what is called *Vairocana* in Sanskrit, meaning "Pervading All Places"—Master Ji of Li stated:
"It penetrates all places and illuminates. As explained extensively above in the five gates, this is the wondrous realm.

This is truly because the three thousand realms are present in a single thought-moment from time immemorial. When a single thought arises, its beginning cannot be fathomed; thus it is called "beginningless.

However, one should further understand that the essence of all Buddha-dharmas is not pervasive, yet it is pervasive; this essence of dharma is neither pervasive nor non-pervasive, yet it pervades the dharma-realm.

The manifestation of realm after realm does not transcend a single thought; because it is the source of numinous awareness, it is called "a single thought.
The mutual generation of land after land does not transcend the Land of Quiescent Light. The Land of Quiescent Light is the essence, while all lands are its function.
Since the function of the mutual generation of lands does not depart from the essence, it is said that they do not transcend the Land of Quiescent Light.

Sentient beings are able to evoke [the response] because they are endowed with the three thousand realms by way of principle. The *Awakening of Faith* states that True Suchness acts as an internal perfuming;

The Buddhas are able to respond because they have fulfilled the three thousand principles; because they fulfill what was not yet fulfilled within those principles, it is called "fulfillment of principles.
On the level of the fruit, the spontaneous compassion that lacks a specific object is such that, though there is no need to respond, they respond as a matter of natural law.
It should be universally pervasive regarding capacities; though the principle of nature is not pervasive, it becomes so through the mutual resonance of the path of response and stimulus.

It is not a mistake. It is like a needle meeting its eye-pin;
otherwise, how could it be like a mirror manifesting images? To illustrate this, I use the metaphor of a mirror manifesting images.
That a mirror possesses the principle of manifesting images is a metaphor for the True and the Responsive.
Form possesses the nature of producing images; the principle-nature truly responding is like a physical form being able to produce a reflection—this is the stage of "principle" (li-ji).
If a single form cannot manifest an image, then the mirror-principle would be exhausted; this passage uses an analogy for the stage of "contemplative practice" (guan-xing-ji).

Although one repeatedly cultivates contemplation, it is likened to a single form facing a bright mirror; because wisdom has not yet attained universal penetration, it is likened to a bright mirror that cannot manifest all images.

As long as there is a mind of effortful application, there will be limits to its commonality. Furthermore, the principle of the exhaustion of conditioned existence (anitya) can be likened to ashes, for it cannot give rise to responsive manifestations. Therefore, it is said that "the principle of the mirror has its limits."

The forms and phenomena have not yet been fully realized. To use an analogy: if they are merely similar [to the reflection] but have not attained the essential nature of the eternally abiding *dharmadhātu*, which is like a bright mirror, then—just as a bright mirror cannot manifest images—the forms and phenomena of the *dharmadhātu* have not yet been fully realized.

If there were a separation between the mirror and [the object], then such a principle might indeed be possible. However, if there is no separation between the impermanent faculty and the permanent mirror, the faculty would not face [the mirror] and thus could not manifest an image;

this is analogous to how a clear mirror cannot reflect a physical form when separated from it. Therefore, it is said that "such a principle might indeed be possible" [only under conditions of separation].

There is no form or object that does not manifest as an image. If the constant mechanism of the rational nature is the true stimulus, then the eternal luminosity of the Dharma-realm is the true response.
This natural interaction of the Way may be illustrated by the worldly example of a bright mirror: there is no form or object that does not appear as an image within it.

If a mirror does not manifest reflections because it is obstructed by dust, and if a worldly copper mirror facing an object fails to manifest reflections because it is necessarily obstructed by fine particles,
so too the rational mirror of the nature cannot manifest the forms of the ten dharma realms because it is obstructed by the dust of the three delusions.
Removing dust depends on human polishing; removing the dust upon a mirror depends on human effort to polish it away.
Likewise, removing the veil of the three delusions depends on the power of contemplation to polish them away.
The manifestation of images is not related to polishing; rather, it is the partial realization of truth up to the ultimate realization of the true nature that is revealed through polishing.
There is the body of wisdom which is realized not through another; it manifests in the ten realms and accords with the principle that they are inherently present, not acquired through cultivation.

This is illustrated by the analogy of the light of a mirror: the copper is inherently present within and does not come from without; therefore, it is said that the manifestation of images is unrelated to polishing.
The meaning is that the ten dharma-realm images are fully contained within the single mind; this is the sense of permanence, not impermanence.
The general principle of observing phenomena through analogies can be understood as seen in the aforementioned notes.

One should know that although the principle is fully possessed both by oneself and others, this is demonstrated in the conclusion as being inherently present within the principle of responsive resonance (*ganying*).

Only then can one, in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), establish the myriad manifestations; this is the establishment of the boundless functioning that accords with the nature.
It does not arise from a self-nature (*svabhāva*). As stated in the preceding text: "The nature is nowhere shifted."
Transformation has no fixed location; because it neither resides within locations nor departs from them, there is no fixed location for self or other.

this is simply the Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind. As for vocal karma, it is movement. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Movement is itself karma;

Regarding the aspect of benefiting others, the activities are divided into three secrets: The Body Secret (*kāyaguhyaka*) is so named because the manifestations of form appear in both large and small dimensions, beyond the comprehension of insentient things.

The Speech Secret (*vāgguhyaka*) is so named because when teaching the Dharma through the sudden or gradual vehicles, those seated together each attain understanding according to their own capacity, yet they do not know one another's realization.
The Mind Secret (*manoguhyaka*) is so named because it discerns the capacities of beings—superior, middling, and inferior—and accords with their respective natures.
Because they attain results without the slightest discrepancy and obtain extraordinary benefits that each remains unaware of the others, it is called the "Secret of Intention" (mantra-guhyaka).
In accordance with the nature of phenomena, names differ; thus, there are the three types of grasses, the two types of trees, and the five vehicles.
The mind-wheel discerns the capacities [of beings]; the power of unconditioned compassion is ever-luminous like a mirror.

they manifest bodies through the supernormal power of bodily transformation.
He preaches the Dharma; with a single voice, he universally responds to the various capacities of sentient beings without the slightest error.

Within the Buddha-body, there is a distinction between the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The *dharmakāya* is called "True," while the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are called "Responsive."

In the classification of the Dharma into the provisional (*upāya*) and the ultimate (*tattva*), that which is employed temporarily according to the capacities of beings is called "provisional," while that which accords with principle and is final is called "ultimate.

If these two explanations were contradictory, why would it be said that "all shall attain the Buddha-way"? One should know that provisional means are reconciled within the ultimate reality; even the slightest merit is not in discord with it.

If there were only the Dharma-body, it would not descend into the world; one should know that the arising of function from the essence is like the sun dividing its form.

The body is itself no-body; the characteristics of the body are ungraspable.

Is it not the case that the hundred realms are one mind, all subsumed within a single thought-moment?

There is no discordance between the provisional and the real; the principle of responding to capacities encompasses both the provisional and the real in their entirety.
Bestowing without moving: without moving from a single thought-moment, one universally responds to all directions.
How could there be any separation or distinction? There is no contradiction with the Great Function.

When speaking in contrast, one establishes the designations of Expedient Means (upāya) and Reality (bhūta); when teaching the Dharma, it is appropriate to accord with the capacities of beings through Expedient Means and Reality.

In terms of the person, one uses the names True Body (dharmakāya) and Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya). Within the essence of numinous awareness, there are fundamentally no such names as "True" or "Responsive."
Things are thus manifested in form.
The principle of the three karmas is identical; this single principle is uniform throughout.
Expedient means and ultimate reality are darkly unified; they accord with reason spontaneously.
This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas; its merit arises from the non-duality of the three karmas.

Regarding the gate of the non-duality of the ten types of recipients being moistened: although the single principle of the conditions for the two benefits of provisional and ultimate [teachings] is the same, the Great and Small Vehicles differ respectively.
This is like the rain from Heaven, which is without distinction, or the vapor of the Earth, which is impartial; the three types of grass and two types of trees simply grow according to their nature.
Although there are differences in the fluctuations of fortune, because the single ground is without distinction, it is called the Gate of Non-duality.

The nature of phenomena is inherently endowed with both the provisional and the real; the innate nature of sentient beings is naturally endowed with the provisional and the real, not something produced through artificial effort.

The beginningless perfuming, whether provisional or real, arises precisely because the nature (*prakṛti*) inherently possesses both the provisional and the real; it is through this perfuming that the nature of the provisional and the real is established.
If there were no perfuming within the nature, the reality (*tathatā*) would not be realized as either provisional or real. Reality itself does not undergo perfuming;
rather, it is only within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) that there exist innate seeds which serve as the internal perfuming for the seventh consciousness and the others.
Because the seeds for the manifestation of the various consciousnesses are newly perfumed, there arises the distinction between the causes and effects of Buddhas and sentient beings,
as well as the difference between defilement and purity; the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* clarifies that True Suchness acts as an internal perfuming,

whereby initial awakening merges with fundamental awakening to function as purity, while deluded consciousness acts as an external perfuming, whereby True Suchness does not maintain its own nature but follows conditions, thus giving rise to the three subtle states.
The six coarse [consciousnesses] arise and perish, functioning as defilement; all such [teachings] are spoken according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Within the Tiantai school, whenever a single dharma arises, one discusses the four teachings: the first three are provisional (upāya), and the last one is real.

Since it is said that the nature is inherently endowed with both the provisional and the real, they do not depend on perfuming to be formed; yet it is also said that they manifest differently upon meeting with perfuming, which does not arise from the nature itself.
Its principles are distinct yet it is resolved through them; its inconceivable nature forms habits in response to conditions.
It is neither provisional nor real, neither true nor false, yet it is simultaneously provisional and real, true and false—it cannot be fathomed by the measures of the ordinary mind.
The provisional and the ultimate, through the principle of perfuming, are eternally equal. If there is a point where perfuming is not permitted, one might ask: "Where does the perfuming reside?

Why was it not perfumed sooner? This too is because the provisional and the ultimate are eternally equal; thus, even without perfuming, they perfume, and the provisional and the ultimate are established as the nature.

When meeting with the opportune conditions, it becomes habitual practice, supported by vows and aspirations. As in the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, his wisdom and vows remained intact and were not lost;
now, such is its nature. If there were no original cause, then a single thought-moment would serve as the original cause.
"Perfuming is also established in vain. "Vain" means empty; it likewise refers to the nature-ground (*prakṛti-bhūmi*).
When encountering perfuming, they naturally differ; what they cultivate is not the same, as the provisional and the real are each received according to their own lot.
This is not due to a difference in nature; for nature is fundamentally a single principle of equality."

Although the nature (*prakṛti*) is without distinction, it must rely upon the manifestation of illusion; through illusory capacity and illusory response, the nature—which is fundamentally without nature—is able to arise in response to conditions.

Therefore, it is said to be "like an illusion," and thus described as "the manifestation of illusion. As the Sūtra says: "True nature is empty of the conditioned; because it arises from conditions, it is like an illusion.
This natural capacity does not manifest until it manifests; hence the *Xuanyan wen* (Profound Text) states: "Capacity (*jī*) means the sense of the subtle; it is the pivot [of response]."

The meanings of "appropriateness" (*yī*) and "fitness" (*yí*) both signify that which can be manifested; here, it is clarified that the wondrous nature of numinous awareness is, by its very dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), capable of being manifested as meaning, spontaneously responding and manifesting illusory transformations in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings.
This constitutes the meaning of "responding to stimuli" (*jìng*).
The capacity to respond to those to be transformed is neither provisional nor ultimate; within the nature of reality, the correspondence between faculty and response is not provisional or ultimate.
However, because the endowment of birth is neither provisional nor ultimate, the innate nature of sentient beings is fundamentally neither provisional nor ultimate.
It accomplishes the capacity for the provisional and the real; it is the capacity that can give rise to the meaning of the provisional and the real.
The Buddha, as the fruition, is also endowed with that which is neither provisional nor real; he has realized the wondrous principle of being neither provisional nor real.
It is the response to the provisional and the real. When there is a capacity [in sentient beings], there is an immediate response. As the ancient text says: "The response accords with the intent;
at that moment, discrimination ceases, yet the illumination of the myriad phenomena remains eternally unmanifest. Therefore, it is said to be the response to the provisional and the real.

The objects and the capacities respond in accordance with one another, and there is no partiality regarding the bodies and lands. Whether the capacities are superior or inferior, the responses are superior or inferior, and the lands are superior or inferior;
the teachings of provisional and ultimate truth are expounded without discrepancy because there is no failure on the part of the capacities. Therefore, it is said that there is no partiality.

The same constant, quiescent light is nothing other than the Dharma-realm. Whether it be the superiority or inferiority of the responsive bodies and lands, all are nothing other than the quiescent light;

furthermore, when the capacity [of the sentient being] is exhausted and the response [of the Buddha] ceases, they both return together to the secret treasury, which is named the "constant, quiescent light" and is fully designated as the Dharma-realm.

Thus we know that the three thousand realms are co-present within the mind-ground, and the three thousand realms of the Buddha’s mind-ground are no different from them. The three thousand realms of both the deluded being and the Buddha are, in their entirety, contained within a single thought-moment.

The four subtle elements (catus-sūkṣma) share the same essence; whether provisional or real, their benefits are equal. These include the four great elements (mahābhūta) and the four subtle elements that constitute form, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Regarding "contact," the preceding text states: "A single atom of retributive form exists together within the Dharma-body of Vairocana.

In the Faxiang school, it is held that from the highest level of the retributive Buddha down to the lowest level of flying birds, all share self-nature (*svabhāva*) as their essence. Nevertheless, it further distinguishes that while self-nature is what language can express, it does not extend to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding that which self-nature can indeed express, the "Chapter on the Three Objects" states: "The objective realm (*viṣaya*) does not follow the mind."
The principles of the provisional teachings of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other schools differ from this reality as much as these distinctions suggest. The purport of this text is as follows:
in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," the three types of grasses and two types of trees, though unequal in their roots, stems, branches, and leaves, all share the same flavor of the earth.

This may be used as a metaphor for the seven vehicles of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), which—though distinct—are in fact nothing other than the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), for they are identical in the single essence of principle.

The *Sārvadharmasiddhi* states that the provisional and the real are inherently equal, and the *Self-Equivalence Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in its own station; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real. By receiving the Dharma of the non-duality of the provisional and the real, one is moistened by that from which it proceeds.
Therefore, through these ten gates, each gate universally enters into matter and mind, and even down to the moisture of sensation; it is thus throughout.
This is because the single principle is equal, such that gate after gate mutually enters and mutually encompasses one another. Thus, one gate contains nine, forming ten gates within each gate;
ten gates constitute a hundred gates, making it clear.

Therefore, the ten wonders (daśa-prakāra-vaipulya) maintain a single principle from beginning to end. Since these ten gates are established based on the ten wonders, their mutual interpenetration arises from the fact that every phenomenon is fundamentally wondrous.
Originally, there are three; originally, these three dharmas are wondrously one. The three dharmas are the nature, which points to the three obstructions;
these obstructions are fundamentally wondrous.
Based on principle, the object is wondrous.
Because it gives rise to understanding and its wisdom is sublime, it is called "wisdom" (jñāna). Referring to this wisdom:
wisdom and understanding guide conduct; because the conduct is sublime, [it is called "conduct"].
Practice and understanding accord with principle; practice and wondrous wisdom wondrously harmonize with the wondrous object.

These three factors correspond to one another—"correspond" (fu) here meaning to join in harmony—thereby achieving the conformity between cultivation and nature, such that the two natures of cultivation and nature become one.

Although they are not different, they appear as different; thus, provisional designations of "shallow" and "deep" are established to set forth their stages. These stages are subtly distinguished in meaning through the six levels of "immediate realization" (*liu ji*).
To avoid confusion and the fear of presumptuously conflating oneself with the supreme sages, it is said that "stages are established to distinguish and eliminate confusion."
The three dharmas and the wondrousness of the three dharmas are simply the realization of those three principles. In some places, the three meanings of "principle" are also mentioned;
however, this refers merely to realizing the wondrousness of the three dharmas—the objects within the cause—upon the basis of the fruit.

The five chapters that follow—the sixth, the wondrousness of resonance; the seventh, the wondrousness of supernormal powers; the eighth, the wondrousness of preaching the Dharma; the ninth, the wondrousness of the retinue;
and the tenth, the wondrousness of benefits—are simply the arising of function from the single principle of the cause and effect of the three dharmas.
The three dharmas give rise to function. It is simply because the fruition is fulfilled that they naturally give rise to function.
Since the "three thousand in a single thought" is established as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the middle, there is function.

Because the wondrous object—the three thousand in a single thought—and the wondrous contemplation—emptiness, provisionality, and the middle—are established, there is function; the object and contemplation merge in profound harmony, resulting in the Great Function.
Thus, inconceivable and wondrous functions are manifested before one.

If one understands this single thought-moment— meaning that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is entirely realized within a single thought-moment— one is a person who has attained sudden enlightenment in the Buddha-vehicle.
The fundamental and manifested traces of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are not remote. It is not only the fundamental and manifested traces of Śākyamuni Buddha alone;

it includes the fundamental and manifested traces of all future Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods, as well as the fundamental and manifested traces of all past and already-gone Buddhas, and the fundamental and manifested traces of all present Buddhas currently existing throughout the ten directions.
At this time, it should be clearly understood that the title designating the "Original" (hon) and the "Trace" (jaku) is indeed trustworthy.

Therefore, I shall restate the ten gates so that the contemplative practice (kan-gyō) may be recognized. Since the title is thus established, these ten gates constitute the interpretation, while the contemplative practice constitutes the application.
The ten gates serve as the dhāraṇī for the contemplative practice; a single thought-moment encompasses the Dharma of the identity of the realm and suchness—this is truly contemplation.
Practitioners must recognize that the title itself is the "wondrous name," which accords with the ten wondrousnesses and ten gates of non-duality of the original and the trace;
thus it is said, "Since this is so.
Viewing the specific as the general, the title serves as the general introduction, while the main body and the circulation section serve as the specific elaboration, restating the ten gates.

The "Phenomenal Characteristics" (xiàng) are called the "Comprehensive Section on Particulars" (lǎn bié mén), as this section gathers and consolidates the subtle contemplations; thus it is called the "Summary" (zǒng).

Furthermore, because the three chapters on Essence, Substance, and Function provide detailed explanations of the three dharmas, they are termed "Comprehensive Particulars. The ten sections are the "Exposition of Names" chapter, which provides a general explanation of the names of the three dharmas, and is thus called the "Summary.
Moreover, the fact that the fundamental and manifested traces of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time differ is what is meant by "Names" (míng).

To survey the particulars within a single thought-moment is not remote; this is called "the general" (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, to explain the characteristics of the realms (*dhātu*) individually, yet for them to be subsumed within a single thought-moment, is called "surveying the particulars as the general.
The general meaning is that the words and phrases of the entire subsequent scripture—from its beginning to its end—do not transcend the title at the outset;
therefore, it is said that "surveying the particulars constitutes the general."
The "Mystic Symbols" (Fuwén) may be understood. Since the phrases following the symbols can be explained according to the titles [of the chapters], they are said to be "knowable.

Furthermore, while the ten gates provide individual explanations of names within the chapter on "Explaining Names" (Shìmíng zhāng), the term "comprehensive" (lǎnbié) refers to the fact that these distinct gates are not dualistic, thus serving as a totality.
Because the titles and the mystic symbols do not diverge into different paths, it is said that "the mystic symbols may be understood."
